faqs.question: What should I write in a Diwali message to my boss?
faqs.answer: One short line: a Diwali wish, one concrete thing from the year, and nothing else. "Happy Diwali, Priya — hope you get a proper break this weekend. Thanks for a good year on the migration work" is the whole message. Under 25 words is the right length.

faqs.question: Is it wrong to send Diwali wishes to my boss?
faqs.answer: No, but the direction matters. Research on ingratiation found it predicted promotability only for some employees under some conditions, so treat an upward greeting as courtesy rather than strategy: no request attached, no praise of their leadership, and send one to your peers the same day.

faqs.question: Should I message colleagues individually or just post in the group?
faqs.answer: Both, split by closeness. Message the four or five people you actually work with by name, and post one original line in the group for everyone else — roughly seven minutes instead of forty. Replying individually to twenty people is not worth it.

faqs.question: When should I send Diwali wishes at work in 2026?
faqs.answer: Friday 6 November 2026, in the afternoon. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November, and the surrounding working days are 6 November and 9–10 November, so the Friday is the last time your message lands in someone's work hours.

faqs.question: Is it okay to send a work Diwali message on the day itself?
faqs.answer: It is allowed but poorly timed. A message arriving at 21:00 on Sunday 8 November lands mid-puja, and one arriving Monday 9 November reads as late. If you do miss the window, switch tense: "Hope Diwali was good" on 10 November is fine.

faqs.question: What should I never say in a Diwali message to a manager?
faqs.answer: Anything about their leadership, guidance, vision or mentorship — that is the line that turns a greeting into flattery. Also leave out any request: a leave approval, an appraisal reminder, or a "let's catch up" ask stapled to a festival wish.

faqs.question: I joined two months ago — should I send Diwali wishes to the team?
faqs.answer: Yes, and say it is your first one here. "First Diwali with this team — thanks for making the last four months easy" does work no generic wish does, because it tells people you noticed them rather than copying a template.

faqs.question: How do I send Diwali wishes to remote colleagues I never speak to?
faqs.answer: Send them a one-line 1:1 message, especially to people two teams over. Microsoft's study of firm-wide remote work found groups became more siloed and communication shifted toward asynchronous email and IM, so a festival greeting is often the only non-work ping of the year.

faqs.question: What do I write if some colleagues do not celebrate Diwali?
faqs.answer: Use "to everyone celebrating" — three words that assume nothing. Note that not-Hindu does not mean not-celebrating: Bandi Chhor Divas falls on 8 November 2026 for Sikh colleagues, and Jain communities mark Diwali too, so guessing from a surname is how this goes wrong.

faqs.question: Does SubhSandesh have a Diwali template for a workplace greeting?
faqs.answer: No. None of the 2,739 pages created since 2026-03-12 across 13 page types is a Diwali page, measured 2026-08-19. The closest existing shape is the Holi greeting page, and for a work audience plain text in the channel colleagues already use is usually better.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Diwali Wishes for Your Boss and Colleagues, Sent by You

Diwali wishes for your boss and colleagues should be two different messages, both sent from your own name rather than forwarded into the team group. Sideways, warmth is enough. Upward, the same warmth carries a risk the research is blunt about: across 92 subordinate–supervisor dyads and 150 triads, ingratiation only predicted promotability for employees high in self-esteem or political skill, and a study of 156 supervisors concluded that ingratiation is useless without helping behaviour behind it. Diwali 2026 falls on Sunday 8 November, so your only sensible work-hours window is Friday 6 November. If you want more than plain text, a shared page is the low-friction option — 51.8% of the 33,007 page views we have recorded open on a phone, and a created page averages 12.1 views, both measured 2026-08-19. Below: six worked messages, the group-chat problem, and the timing.

## What makes the message to your boss a different message

An upward festival greeting is a status-crossing phatic message: its job is to maintain a relationship, not to transfer information. The same eleven words read as friendly from a peer and calculating from a subordinate, because the relationship does most of the interpreting.

A 2025 analysis of WhatsApp exchanges in the [ACROSS Journal of Interdisciplinary Cross-Border Studies](https://gup.ugal.ro/ugaljournals/index.php/across/article/view/7375) found that the phatic tokens people use differ systematically between solidarity relationships and status-differential ones. The four rules below make that difference deliberate.

- **Attach no request.** Not a leave approval, not a reminder about your appraisal, not "let's catch up when you're back". A Diwali message with an ask stapled to it is a request wearing a diya.
- **Say nothing about their leadership.** "Your guidance lights our path" is the most common line in the corporate-wishes lists, and the one that marks a message as flattery. [Ingratiation predicted promotability](https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/items/431efb08-2008-4326-886b-c6a17f1be91a) in only some conditions across two studies (2013), so the upside is not reliable enough to risk it.
- **Keep it under 25 words.** Length reads as effort, and effort directed only upward is what observers notice.
- **Send one to your peers too, the same day.** Warmth aimed exclusively up the hierarchy is the pattern people find distasteful; the same warmth spread sideways reads as ordinary courtesy.

The [Intangible Capital study of 156 supervisors and 453 subordinates](https://www.intangiblecapital.org/index.php/ic/article/view/759) across 35 hotels in Islamabad (2016) is the useful corrective here: ingratiation raised supervisor satisfaction only through actual helping behaviour, and the authors concluded plainly that ingratiation is useless without it. A good Diwali message cannot substitute for a year of work. It can only avoid spoiling one.

## The team group problem, and whether to reply to twenty people individually

By 07:00 on 8 November the team WhatsApp group will hold twenty forwarded images, most of them the same temple-and-diya stock photos in a different font. Nobody dislikes them and nobody remembers them, because a forward carries no marker of the relationship it travelled through.

The realistic answer to "should I message all twenty individually?" is no. Message the four or five people you actually work with by name, and post one line of your own in the group for everyone else — written by you, not forwarded. That is roughly seven minutes of work versus forty.

One line naming something specific from the year beats twenty identical forwards, because it is the only message in the thread nobody else could have sent.

## Six Diwali messages for six recipients

Copy the shape, then replace the specifics. A message that names nothing specific is a forward with extra steps.

### 1. Your direct manager
**Send:** 1:1 chat, Friday 6 November afternoon. **Message:** "Happy Diwali, Priya — hope you get a proper break with family this weekend. Thanks for a good year on the migration work." **Why it works:** it names one real thing, carries no request, and comments on the project rather than on her leadership. **Leave out:** guidance, vision, mentorship, "under your leadership".

### 2. Your skip-level
**Send:** email or 1:1 chat, Friday 6 November. **Message:** "Wishing you and your family a happy Diwali, Sir/Anil — enjoy the break." **Why it works:** at two levels of distance shorter is safer; a long message to someone who does not manage your work is the clearest ingratiation signal there is. **Leave out:** project detail they lack context for, and any hint that you want more visibility.

### 3. A peer you are close to
**Send:** 1:1 chat, any time from 6 November. **Message:** "Happy Diwali! Don't eat all the kaju katli in one sitting like last year. Say hi to your parents from me." **Why it works:** the silly specific detail proves the message was written for one person. **Leave out:** prosperity, success, milestones — nobody talks to a friend like a greeting card.

### 4. A peer you barely know
**Send:** 1:1 chat, Friday 6 November. **Message:** "Happy Diwali, Rohit — hope you have a good few days off." **Why it works:** low warmth is correct; an over-familiar message to someone you have spoken to twice is more awkward than a short one. **Leave out:** their family, their plans, any implied closeness.

### 5. Someone who reports to you
**Send:** 1:1, Friday 6 November, before you send anything to your own manager. **Message:** "Happy Diwali, Sneha. Switch off properly — the dashboard can wait until Tuesday." **Why it works:** permission to disconnect beats good wishes, and sending down before sending up fixes the asymmetry at its root. **Leave out:** performance talk, however positive.

### 6. The team group
**Send:** one message, Friday 6 November, late afternoon. **Message:** "Happy Diwali to everyone celebrating, and a good long weekend to everyone who isn't. Genuinely good year, this one — thanks all." **Why it works:** one original line, one inclusive clause, no image. **Leave out:** the forward. Also the @everyone tag.

## Five ways to send it, compared

Five delivery routes, and what each costs for a twenty-person team.

| Option | Time for 20 colleagues | Personalisation | What the evidence says |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forwarded image in the team group | Under 1 minute | None | Carries no relationship marker (ACROSS, 2025) |
| One line of your own in the group | 2 minutes | Team-level only | The only message in the thread nobody else could send |
| 1:1 text to each person | 25–40 minutes | Name plus one detail | Worth it for the 4–5 you work with daily |
| Email to the whole team | 5 minutes | Salutation only | Reads as an announcement, not a greeting |
| A shared personalised page, one link | ~15 minutes to build | Photo, name, message | 51.8% of our 33,007 recorded views open on a phone; 12.1 views per page — measured 2026-08-19 |

Personalise for the handful who matter and use one honest group line for the rest. Volume is not the variable that helps.

## Timing: Diwali 2026 falls on Sunday 8 November

The five days run 6–10 November 2026, with Lakshmi Puja on Sunday 8 November. That makes 6 November a Friday, and 9–10 November a Monday and Tuesday — so the festival day itself sits in nobody's working hours.

Send on Friday 6 November, in the afternoon. A greeting arriving at 21:00 on Sunday, mid-puja, is an interruption; one arriving at 09:00 on Monday 9 November is late in the way everyone notices.

If you do miss it, switch tense rather than apologising: "Hope Diwali was good" on Tuesday 10 November is fine. "Sorry for the late wishes" turns a two-line greeting into a small confession.

## First Diwali at the company, fifth Diwali, and the remote colleague

A first-Diwali-here message should say so: "First Diwali with this team — thanks for making the last four months easy." That sentence does work no generic wish does. At five years in the opposite applies: you have history, so use it and drop the introductions.

For distributed teams, the greeting is doing structural work. Microsoft's study of firm-wide remote work, published in *Nature Human Behaviour* in September 2021, found the shift made formal groups and informal community structures [more siloed](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-effects-of-remote-work-on-collaboration-among-information-workers/), cut total meeting and call hours by 5% of the pre-pandemic level, and pushed communication toward asynchronous email and instant messaging.

In that setting a Diwali message may be the only non-work ping a remote colleague gets from you all year. Send it to the people two teams over you never have a reason to call — precisely the tie siloing removes.

## One line that covers a mixed team

Your colleague list is mixed, so "to everyone celebrating" is the construction that does not misfire. It costs three words and assumes nothing.

Note also that "not Hindu" is not the same as "not celebrating". The University of Saskatchewan's multi-faith calendar lists [Bandi Chhor Divas on 8 November 2026](https://students.usask.ca/academic-calendar/2026/11/08-mfo-bandi-chhor-divas.php), the Sikh observance falling on the same day, and Jain communities mark Diwali too. Guessing from a surname is how you get this wrong; the inclusive clause means you never have to guess.

## When to skip the Diwali message at work

Skip it if you are three days from an appraisal conversation or a raise request with that manager. The message will be read backwards through the ask, and the research on conditional ingratiation effects suggests you gain nothing.

Skip it if the person has had a bereavement this year; a separate call is the better move. Skip the group post if your last group message was a complaint about workload — the whiplash is worse than silence.

And a limitation worth stating plainly: **SubhSandesh has no Diwali template today.** Of 2,739 pages created since 2026-03-12 across 13 page types, none is a Diwali page. If you want a shareable festival greeting page you can browse the [full SubhSandesh template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates), and the closest existing shape is the [Holi festival greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/holi) — a festival greeting page with the wrong festival on it. For a work audience, plain text in the channel they already use is usually the better call.

## Sources

- [Getting Ahead Through Flattery: Ingratiation and Promotability](https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/items/431efb08-2008-4326-886b-c6a17f1be91a) — Sibunruang, Capezio & Restubog, *Journal of Career Assessment*, 2013 (abstract read; full text restricted).
- [Effect of Ingratiation on Supervisor Satisfaction Through Helping Behavior](https://www.intangiblecapital.org/index.php/ic/article/view/759) — Asadullah et al., *Intangible Capital* 12(5), 2016, open access.
- [Beyond Words: Phatic Communication in Instant Messaging](https://gup.ugal.ro/ugaljournals/index.php/across/article/view/7375) — Toma, *ACROSS Journal of Interdisciplinary Cross-Border Studies* 8(2), 27 March 2025 (abstract read).
- [The Effects of Remote Work on Collaboration Among Information Workers](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-effects-of-remote-work-on-collaboration-among-information-workers/) — Yang et al., *Nature Human Behaviour*, September 2021 (summary read; journal text paywalled).
- [Bandi Chhor Divas, 8 November 2026](https://students.usask.ca/academic-calendar/2026/11/08-mfo-bandi-chhor-divas.php) — University of Saskatchewan multi-faith observances calendar.

failed.why: The six worked-message blocks under H3s each run to four sentences because they carry four labelled fields (Send / Message / Why it works / Leave out) in one paragraph. Splitting them into separate lines would double the section's length and push the body over 1,800 words; the rest of the post holds to 2–3 sentences.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this query written bottom-up, and the only one that names the ingratiation research, answers the twenty-forwards question with a time cost, and states that Diwali 2026 lands on a Sunday when nobody is working — none of the five competitor pages does any of that. Two caveats: the table's first-party column carries our numbers in one row rather than all five, since we hold no data on WhatsApp or email sends; and segmenting by recipient is a convention the wishes farms already use, so the divergence is in the framing and the 'leave out' field, not the shape. Domain authority against fnp/floweraura-class retailers and HR-platform blogs is the real constraint, and that takes months, not phrasing.
